The HTA Verification Framework

Source: vignettes/verification-framework.Rmd
verification-framework.Rmd
library(testhta)
library(testthat)

1. Hierarchy of Testing in Health Economic Modelling

Testing can be performed at different levels of abstraction. Adapted from the software engineering Test Pyramid framework (Cohn, 2009), automated checks in health economic modelling are organized into three structural tiers:

  1. Level 1: Unit Testing (Lowest Level — Fast, High Isolation)
    Isolates the smallest testable parts of an application (“units”)—typically a single, self-contained helper function—and verifies that they function correctly (e.g., a function that converts a rate to a probability, applies a discount factor, or draws a parameter sample).
  2. Level 2: Integration Testing (Middle Level — Subcomponent Interaction)
    Verifies that multiple components (input structures, transition matrices, simulation loops, and summary extractors) interact correctly to produce logically sound results. Because health economic models frequently lack a simple “test oracle” for complex multi-state traces, executing run_model() under controlled boundary conditions to check summary outputs like QALYs, Life Expectancy (LE), and ICERs primarily operates at this integration level.
  3. Level 3: System or End-to-End Testing (Highest Level — Full Pipeline)
    Executes the entire decision-analytic pipeline from raw data ingestion to final policy outputs (e.g., running a 10,000-iteration Probabilistic Sensitivity Analysis (PSA) pipeline to verify that it completes without memory leaks, handles missing data gracefully, and outputs a valid ICER and CEAC).

2. Why Use testthat Instead of Ad-Hoc Console Checks?

The testthat package (Wickham, 2011) is the standard framework for automated testing in R. To set up an R package or project to use testthat (edition 3), run:

usethis::use_testthat(3)

This creates the tests/testthat/ directory and tests/testthat.R runner script. Automated checks in testthat are written as expectations (functions starting with expect_, such as expect_equal(), expect_lt(), expect_gt(), expect_true()) grouped inside test_that("<description>", { ... }) blocks.

Unlike ad-hoc console checks using raw operators (== 0 or <), which return a generic FALSE or fail silently unless manually inspected each time a script is run, testthat expectations act as automated diagnostic tools. When an expectation fails, testthat immediately flags the exact test requirement ID, file, line number, and numerical discrepancy between actual and expected values.

3. Health Economic Modelling Test Suite (T01 – T12)

Table 1 below presents the standardized suite of 12 verification tests, extreme-value checks, and logical assertions adapted from established HTA quality-assurance frameworks:

  • Internal consistency and extreme-value checks (McCabe & Dixon, 2000)
  • Comprehensive “black-box” verification criteria (Tappenden & Chilcott, 2014)
  • Automated decision-analytic checking principles (Dasbach & Elbasha, 2017)
  • Technical verification standards reinforced by the CHEERS statement (Husereau et al., 2013)
ID Group Test Condition Expected Result
T01 Population Treatment effect the same for all treatments, e.g., Set relative treatment effects (OR, HR, RR) =1= 1 All treatments produce equal estimates of total LYGs and total QALYs
T02 Population Set mortality rates (or corresponding transition probabilities) =0= 0 LE=time horizon\text{LE} = \text{time horizon} (assuming a fixed, finite time horizon to avoid an infinite loop)
T03 Population Set mortality rates (or corresponding transition probabilities) to produce a probability of 11 LE=1 cycle\text{LE} = 1\text{ cycle} (or 0.50.5 depending on within-cycle correction implementation)
T04 QALY Set discount rate =0= 0 (assuming utility =1= 1 for all living health states) Total QALYs equal LE
T05 QALY Set all living health state utility parameters =1= 1 QALY gains exactly equal LYGs
T06 QALY Apply standard positive discount rate vs. 00 rate Discounted QALYs<undiscounted QALYs ∀ treatments\text{Discounted QALYs} < \text{undiscounted QALYs } \forall \text{ treatments}
T07 QALY Set QALY discount rate =∞= \infty QALY gains after time 00 equal zero
T08 Cost Set intervention costs =0= 0 ICER is reduced†^\dagger
T09 Cost Increase intervention costs ICER is increased†^\dagger
T10 Cost Set cost discount rate =0= 0 Total costs equal the raw arithmetic sum of unadjusted state costs ∀\forall treatments (and discounted costs << undiscounted costs)
T11 Cost Set cost discount rate =∞= \infty Costs after time 00 equal zero
T12 Input Sample parameters from probabilistic distributions Range of sampled values does not violate distribution boundaries, NaNs, or critical numerical precision errors

†^\daggerNote on ICER Directionality (T08 & T09): Assuming a controlled test environment where baseline Incremental Effects (IE\text{IE}) are known to be strictly positive (IE>0\text{IE} > 0). In testthat, this assumption can be guarded explicitly using testthat::skip_if_not(inc_qalys > 0, ...). If evaluating a scenario with negative incremental health effects, the verification logic should isolate Incremental Costs (IC\text{IC}) instead.

Note on Within-Cycle Correction (T03): In models applying a standard half-cycle (or within-cycle) correction, setting mortality to 100%100\% in the first cycle will conceptually result in a life expectancy of 0.50.5 cycles rather than 1.01.0 cycle.

  2. Wickham, H. (2011). testthat: Get Started with Testing. The R Journal, 3, 5–10.
